sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Tinnitus is a highly prevalent and distressing symptom in patients with idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (ISSNHL). While international clinical guidelines primarily focus on hearing recovery through pharmacological interventions, effective treatment for tinnitus remains limited. Sound therapy, such as masking and retraining therapy, has emerged as a promising treatment. This systematic review aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of sound therapy for the alleviation of tinnitus in adult patients with ISSNHL.

sec.title: Methods and analysis
sec.p: Researchers will independently conduct searches for randomised controlled trials in the following databases: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), CNKI and Wanfang Data. The literature search is scheduled for March 2026 without language restrictions. The review will include studies involving adult patients (18 years or older) diagnosed with ISSNHL with tinnitus symptoms who underwent sound therapy (including Tinnitus Masking Therapy, Tinnitus Retraining Therapy or music therapy) with standard drug therapy, placebo or any other non-acoustic interventions compared with the same treatment alone. Researchers will independently screen studies, extract data and assess the risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Data analyses will be performed using RevMan V.10.0.2 and Stata V.18.0 software. The certainty of the evidence will be evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: This study relies on the analysis of secondary data from previously published trials; therefore, ethical approval from a research ethics committee is not required. The results of this systematic review will be disseminated through publication in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

caption.title: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

list-item.p: The review will be according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines.

The certainty of evidence will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach to ensure high methodological standards.
Study selection, data extraction and risk of bias assessment will be performed independently by two reviewers, with arbitration by a third reviewer when required.
Clinical and methodological heterogeneity across sound therapy modalities, treatment timing and outcome measures may limit the comparability of included studies.
The restriction to randomised controlled trials may reduce the number of eligible studies and limit the certainty of pooled estimates.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (ISSNHL) is defined as a sensorineural hearing loss of unknown cause within a 72-hour period. It is characterised by a hearing reduction of at least 30 decibels (dB) across three or more contiguous frequencies and is often accompanied by tinnitus and/or vertigo.1

Tinnitus is a common accompanying symptom of ISSNHL, with a reported prevalence ranging from 78.2% to 91.0%.2 In the absence of timely treatment, patients may suffer from persistent hearing loss and tinnitus. Although tinnitus symptoms often ameliorate alongside hearing recovery following conventional treatment, a subset of patients may experience permanent tinnitus.35 This residual tinnitus imposes a significant economic burden and may exacerbate the psychological and functional distress associated with hearing loss.6 7

The first-line treatment for ISSNHL involves systemic corticosteroids, which can significantly improve hearing level.8 9 It is worth noting that international guidelines provide limited recommendations for the management of acute and residual tinnitus associated with ISSNHL.1 10 11

To date, there is no specific cure for tinnitus, and most clinical guidelines do not recommend pharmacological interventions.61214 Furthermore, hearing aids and implantable devices are often costly and demonstrate uncertain efficacy.15 Consequently, sound therapy, also known as acoustic therapy, is a commonly used therapeutic approach.

Sound therapy is broadly defined as the clinical use of sound to modify the perception and/or reactions to tinnitus.6 It offers the benefits of effectively alleviating tinnitus symptoms while being non-invasive and having a favourable safety profile.1618

Sound therapy involves Tinnitus Masking Therapy (TMT), Tinnitus Retraining Therapy (TRT), music therapy, etc. TMT primarily relies on broadband noise to generate a masking effect, with the dual goals of inducing tinnitus relief and promoting habituation.6 TRT is based on the neurophysiological model of tinnitus, which aims to improve patient tolerance and habituation to the tinnitus signal. It consists of two main components: sound maskers and educational counselling.6

Although recent studies have explored the use of sound therapy for tinnitus associated with ISSNHL,1921 there is currently no systematic review or meta-analysis examining its efficacy in this specific population. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy of sound therapy for ISSNHL-associated tinnitus.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: The principal objective of this systematic review is to evaluate the effect of sound therapy on tinnitus in ISSNHL of adult patients.

sec.title: Methods and analysis
sec.p: The design and reporting of this study were developed in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines.22

sec.title: Data sources and search strategy
sec.p: We will search for articles in the following electronic databases: PubMed, Embase, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science (WOS), ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP), China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) and Wanfang Data.

The search terms will include ‘Sudden Hearing Loss’, ‘Tinnitus’, ‘Acoustic Therapy’, ‘Sound Therapy’, ‘Masking’, ‘Tinnitus Retraining Therapy’ and ‘Music Therapy’. Corresponding Chinese search terms will be used for the Chinese databases. The search will be without language restrictions. Detailed search strategies are presented in online supplemental file 1. The literature search is scheduled for March 2026. All retrieved records will be imported into EndNote X9 software for management and screening, and duplicate records will be confirmed and eliminated.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Two researchers (R-QY and Y-H), who are trained in systematic review methodology, will independently screen the titles and abstracts of all potentially suitable articles. Subsequently, the full texts of the selected articles will be carefully reviewed to determine which meet the inclusion criteria.
If consensus cannot be reached, a third researcher (L-HP) will make the final decision on study inclusion.
Specific reasons for exclusion at the full-text screening stage will be documented. The study selection process and reasons for exclusion will be illustrated in a PRISMA flow diagram (figure 1).

sec.title: Type of participant
sec.p: This study, with no restrictions on gender, will include adult patients aged 18 years or older diagnosed with ISSNHL accompanied by tinnitus.
We will accept a diagnosis of ISSNHL based on national or international guidelines.1 10 11
Patients with conductive or mixed hearing loss, as well as tinnitus resulting from other etiologies (eg, noise-induced hearing loss, presbycusis or Meniere’s disease), will be excluded.

sec.title: Type of interventions
sec.p: Sound therapy combined with standard drug therapy, placebo, or any other non-acoustic interventions.
Sound therapy (begins within 6 months of onset, the duration ≤6 months): TMT, TRT and other sound therapy (eg, music therapy).

sec.title: Type of comparator
sec.p: Use of standard drug therapy, placebo, or any other non-acoustic interventions.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: Studies will not be excluded based on the choice of tinnitus-related outcome measures, provided validated instruments are utilised.

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: The primary outcome is tinnitus symptom severity, defined as the reduction in tinnitus-related distress and handicap and tinnitus perception using measures such as Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI),23 Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI)24 and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS).

sec.title: Secondary outcomes
sec.p: The secondary outcome is hearing recovery, defined as the change in pure-tone thresholds and speech discrimination.

Additional secondary outcomes involve the evaluation of psychological outcomes and life quality, assessed using validated instruments such as the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), 36-Item Short Form Survey (SF-36) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI).
Adverse events: incidence and severity of treatment-related adverse events.

sec.title: Types of studies
sec.p: This systematic review will include randomised controlled trials (including parallel-group and crossover designs) evaluating the efficacy of sound therapy for tinnitus in ISSNHL.
Non-randomised studies and observational study designs (such as cohort, case–control, case series and case report studies) will be excluded.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Two researchers (R-QY and Y-H) will independently extract data using a self-developed data extraction form. The extracted data will include:

list-item.p: Study characteristics: first author, journal, year of publication and study design.
Patient characteristics: sample size per group, age, gender and severity of hearing loss.
Interventions: types of sound therapy, frequency and duration of treatment.
Outcomes: primary and secondary outcome data.

sec.p: On completion of the extraction process, the two data sets will be cross-checked and merged. Any disagreement will be resolved through discussion with a third researcher (L-HP). If necessary, we will contact the corresponding authors via email or telephone to request missing data or supplementary information regarding assessment scales. If sufficient information cannot be obtained, we will analyse the available data.

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: Two researchers (T-HQ and H-YC) will independently assess the risk of bias for the included studies using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool.25 We will evaluate multiple sources of bias, including the randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome and selection of the reported result. The overall risk of bias for each study will be graded as ‘Low Risk’, ‘Some Concerns’ (or ‘Unclear Risk’) or ‘High Risk’. The rationale for these judgements will be documented in a risk-of-bias table. Disagreements will be resolved primarily through discussion between the two reviewers; if a consensus cannot be reached, a third reviewer (T-L) will provide a final decision.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: We will analyse the data using RevMan V.10.0.2 (https://revman.cochrane.org/) and Stata 18 software.

sec.title: Measures of treatment effect
sec.p: Dichotomous outcomes will be expressed as risk ratios with 95% CIs. Continuous outcomes will be expressed as mean differences with 95% CIs if the measurement units are consistent, or as standardised mean differences with 95% CIs if different measurement scales are used.

sec.title: Assessment of heterogeneity
sec.p: Cochran’s Q test and the I² statistic will be used to assess heterogeneity among the included studies.26 For the Q statistic, a p value<0.05 will be considered statistically significant. For the I² statistic, I² < 25% indicates insignificant heterogeneity; values between 25% and 50% indicate moderate heterogeneity; and I² > 50% indicates substantial heterogeneity. Given the anticipated clinical heterogeneity across the different types of sound therapy and treatment protocols, a random-effects model will be used as the default approach.

sec.title: Additional analyses
sec.p: We will conduct sensitivity analyses, meta-regression and subgroup analyses based on various study characteristics—such as type of intervention, study design, study location, study quality, participant characteristics, timing of intervention (eg, ≤1 month vs >1 month postonset), duration of intervention (eg, <3 months vs ≥3 months) and the age of patients and the age of patients.
Especially, subgroup analyses for different sound therapies will be performed to examine potential heterogeneity in treatment effect, where sufficient data are available. Subgroups will include:

list-item.p: Comprehensive protocols (eg, TRT + educational counselling and/or psychological intervention).

sec.p: If the extracted data are insufficient for a quantitative meta-analysis, a qualitative synthesis will be performed.

sec.title: Assessment of reporting biases
sec.p: Publication bias will be assessed by visual inspection of funnel plots when 10 or more studies are included in the analysis. We will assess funnel plot symmetry using Begg’s and Egger’s tests, with a significance level of p<0.10. The potential impact of publication bias on the effect size will be evaluated using the trim-and-fill method.

sec.title: Quality of evidence
sec.p: The quality of evidence for included studies will be evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.27 Reviewers will consider risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. The quality of evidence will be graded as high, moderate, low or very low.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: We intend to publish this systematic review in a peer-reviewed journal. Our findings will provide evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of acoustic therapy for tinnitus associated with sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Ethical approval is not required for this review as it does not involve direct participation by human subjects.
